# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review of Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management

## Introduction and Epidemiology
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a life-threatening form of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction that affects women late in pregnancy or in the early postpartum months [1,2]. Defined as an idiopathic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) typically below 45% [1,2], PPCM remains a primary cause of maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide [3,4]. The incidence varies substantially by geographic region, with major risk factors including advanced maternal age, multiparity, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and preeclampsia [3,4].

## Pathophysiology
The precise etiology of PPCM was long considered enigmatic, but recent preclinical and clinical investigations have elucidated a multi-hit vascular and hormonal pathway [5,6]. Under high oxidative stress conditions in the late-gestational heart, the lysosomal protease cathepsin D is upregulated, cleaving the nursing hormone prolactin into a toxic 16-kilodon (16-kDa) fragment [5]. This 16-kDa prolactin fragment promotes endothelial cell apoptosis and disrupts cardiomyocyte metabolism [5]. Simultaneously, late-pregnancy secretion of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt1) by the placenta neutralizes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), exacerbating systemic endothelial dysfunction [6]. Importantly, a genetic predisposition also underpins PPCM [7,8]. Approximately 10% to 15% of patients carry truncating mutations in the titin gene (*TTN*), suggesting that PPCM may represent a manifestation of subclinical dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) unmasked by the hemodynamic stress of late pregnancy [7,8].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis
PPCM typically presents in the first postpartum month [9,10]. Symptoms frequently mimic common third-trimester physiological complaints, such as dyspnea, orthopnea, and peripheral edema, leading to diagnostic delays [9,10]. Biomarkers and proof-of-concept pilot studies have historically shown that elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines and brain natriuretic peptides can assist in early identification [11,12]. Diagnostic evaluation of suspected PPCM is characterized by persistent left ventricular impairment and myocardial stress, as shown in large European and North American cohorts [13,14]. Modern clinical databases have demonstrated that standard diagnostic protocols must immediately exclude other causes of heart failure [14,15].

## Therapeutic Management
Management of PPCM requires a multidisciplinary cardio-obstetric approach [14,15]. Pre-delivery, standard heart failure guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) must be modified to protect the fetus: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) are strictly contraindicated [14,15]. Post-delivery, standard GDMT can be safely titrated [15]. 

Targeting the pathogenic prolactin pathway has emerged as a disease-specific breakthrough [16]. The dopamine agonist bromocriptine, which suppresses pituitary prolactin secretion, has demonstrated efficacy in improving LVEF recovery in clinical trials [11,16]. Standard protocols recommend bromocriptine paired with anticoagulation to counter the prothrombotic state associated with prolactin inhibition [16]. For patients presenting with severe cardiogenic shock or life-threatening arrhythmias, temporary mechanical support or a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD) may be utilized during the high-risk early post-diagnosis period [17,18].

## Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancy
PPCM is associated with a higher rate of myocardial recovery compared to other cardiomyopathies, with approximately 50% to 70% of patients recovering normal LVEF [10,19]. However, subsequent pregnancies pose unique and serious challenges [20,21]. Patients with persistent left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF < 50%) must be strongly counseled against future pregnancies due to an extremely high risk of clinical deterioration and mortality [20,21]. Even in women who achieve full myocardial recovery, a significant risk of recurrence remains [21,22]. Detailed clinical guidelines and critical assessments of heart failure in pregnancy emphasize the need for close monitoring [23,24]. Echocardiographic evaluation remains fundamental for identifying those at risk of long-term impairment [25].

## Global Perspectives and Guidelines
Recent studies have evaluated the integration of bromocriptine therapy across diverse medical environments, reinforcing its utility [26]. Global registries and reviews stress that PPCM is a worldwide healthcare burden requiring unified diagnostic and management parameters [27,28]. Accordingly, the 2018 European Society of Cardiology guidelines and associated clinical reviews outline clear management algorithms during and after pregnancy [29,30]. Together, these advances highlight the critical need for early diagnosis, optimal pharmacological intervention, and structured risk assessment to protect both mother and child.
